questions.q: What tradeoff does shrinkage estimation exploit when estimating a covariance matrix?
options: It trades computation time for accuracy
It trades a small amount of bias (by blending toward a structured target) for a reduction in estimation variance, lowering total expected error
It eliminates the need for any historical data
It trades memory usage for speed
questions.explain: Shrinkage estimators are deliberately biased when delta>0, but the reduction in variance can lower the total expected error (bias squared plus variance) relative to the unbiased sample covariance.

questions.q: What target does Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage blend the sample covariance toward, and how is the shrinkage intensity chosen?
options: A random matrix; intensity is chosen arbitrarily
A scaled-identity matrix; the shrinkage intensity is computed directly from the data to be approximately optimal
The previous month's covariance matrix; intensity is fixed at 0.5
A zero matrix; intensity must be set manually by the user
questions.explain: Ledoit-Wolf shrinks toward a scaled-identity target and computes a data-driven shrinkage intensity, larger when the sample covariance is noisier relative to the target's structure.

questions.q: In the worked example, the Ledoit-Wolf estimate had a Frobenius error vs. the TRUE covariance of 0.00831, slightly worse than the sample covariance's 0.00768. What does this illustrate?
options: Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage is never useful
The code must contain a bug

Shrinking toward an identity-like target doesn't always get literally closer to a true matrix with its own factor structure -- shrinkage's real payoff can show up elsewhere, like out-of-sample behavior
Shrinkage always increases Frobenius error relative to the sample covariance in every case
questions.explain: The guide notes this as a reminder that closeness to the true matrix in one sample isn't shrinkage's only or most important benefit -- out-of-sample likelihood told a different story.

questions.q: What happened to the condition number when Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage was applied in the worked example?
options: It increased from 261.9 to 1125.5
It stayed exactly the same
It dropped by more than 4x, from 1125.5 (sample) to 261.9 (Ledoit-Wolf), with only a 0.076 shrinkage intensity
It became undefined
questions.explain: Even a small shrinkage intensity of 0.076 reduced the condition number by more than 4x, making the matrix far more numerically stable to invert.

questions.q: On the held-out test sample, how did the Ledoit-Wolf covariance estimate compare to the sample covariance in average negative log-likelihood?
options: Ledoit-Wolf scored substantially better (-154.79 vs. -110.21, lower being better), despite being further from the true matrix in Frobenius distance on the training sample
They scored identically
The sample covariance scored better out-of-sample
Negative log-likelihood cannot be computed for covariance matrices
questions.explain: Ledoit-Wolf's out-of-sample negative log-likelihood (-154.79) was substantially better than the sample covariance's (-110.21), showing shrinkage's bias-variance tradeoff paying off where it matters most -- generalization.
